notes.title: Developers diaries #12+1
notes.content:
We have never described the development sequence in the format of logs: what we did, how our work is progressing, and what will happen next. Only one of the logs was dedicated to how we started developing City Car Driving.

As was noted in the tenth log, we came to creating the game gradually: we collected various build options, tested engines.

In this log, we will talk about how we are working on CCD 2.0 after we have completed work with the prototype: how many people are in the team, what we have fully implemented, and what we is still in the making. 

After we got the prototype and confirmation for us that CCD 2.0 could be created, the very first thing we decided to create from scratch was the setting. We realized that many players expected an update to the first part, but we wanted to provide something new.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/4fa3ab765c1120603bf5806d76a962f6a95a5dd6.png[/img]
[h2]Setting | Location[/h2]
The very first thing our small team started to do was to conceptualize the main location that will open CCD 2.0. 

Of the many options, we chose the average option in the south of the Mediterranean with European traffic rules.

We made that decision because we wanted to reinvent the core CCD gaming formula.
The setting of the original CCD is Russia. Regardless of the change in the traffic rule base in the settings, the location did not change.

We didn’t really like this – it contradicted the first principle developed for us: everything should be authentic and not take away from the gameplay.

It is precisely because of the combination of our approach and the desire to try something new that CCD 2.0 opens in a Mediterranean location where it is eternal summer.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/743dcd6699aded6a34a86a6fad3624c7d14e7fd5.png[/img]
At the same time, we realize that you are not likely to want to study the traffic rules of a specific country in which most players do not live. European road safety rules are very universal: they are similar to many rules in countries around the world (except for unique ones, such as Great Britain, for example), and in our idea, they should suit most players.

In the future, we plan to expand and add game locations: move from the abstract “European Mediterranean countries” to specific ones.

During development, we saw all your feedback, so the first thing we want to add is Russia. Only after the European and Russian regions are fully implemented, will we think about expanding the in-game geography.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
Before we began to talk in detail in our Logs about what we were developing, it seemed that we were literally taking the original CCD, transferring it to a modern engine, remaking favorite locations and that’s it. In fact, along with developing the location, we designed the gameplay.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/694d9e029f93108362ccf38ec54f0e3dc7a64188.png[/img]
Combining two game modes into one turned the entire gameplay into one campaign. That entailed abandoning the capability for the player to customize the amount and density of traffic. Abandoning the free choice of weather conditions and time.

Instead, we are developing an environment that simulates a complete game world with its own rules and dynamic changes in weather and traffic. 

In addition to global changes in the weather, we reduced the scope of the driving school. CCD 2.0 retains the core exercises and exam. However, during development we removed many exercises. That needed to be compensated for with something: that’s how the “Quest Exercises” appeared. Cargo transportation is a logical continuation of what was in the original CCD. 

Also, all the infrastructure relevant to driving has been added.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/4dade8553fbb94f0a68acc95d1cd6a42790e9c6d.png[/img]
[h2]Team | How things are now[/h2]
Of course, in words, in the form of a small story, it looks like an excellent car simulator. Let’s go through the key points of the project in reality.

The concept of the gameplay, location, and basic mechanics was completed in mid-2022. After that, we started development.

By the start of 2023, we had the location and several basic mechanics roughly ready. We expected that we would be able to quickly talk about the development of the project, but our silence lasted for long six months: this is due to the fact that we put some of the mechanics on the back burner (we haven’t talked about them yet, everything mentioned in the logs will be available in the game). Part of the location also had to be removed.

Realizing that we had kept silent for too long, we filmed driving a car on the most finished street in the game: this became the first teaser for the game.

Then and now we did not start an advertising campaign. We share the development with the audience that we gathered over the years of the life of the original CCD and carefully select all the feedback; at this pace, we can create what we planned, manage to make changes to the project, and lay down opportunities for the future. 

After a long time of development, we decided to share a little information about ourselves, and at what stage our development is.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/4f5edf731c37fa56498da1543c46ab3dff45e879.png[/img]
[b]How many people are there on the team?[/b]
[i]Currently fifteen. Initially, CCD 2.0 was developed by no more than three.[/i] 

[b]How long has CCD 2.0 been in development?[/b]
[i]One and half year; before this, research was carried out, various prototypes were created.[/i]

[b]Is this a simulator or a game?[/b]
[i]Despite the fact that we are Forward and are developing City Car Driving 2.0, we are a separate division from the simulators and are creating specifically a game.[/i]

[b]Why will the game be released in early access?[/b] 
[i]We don’t have the budget to create a large-scale car simulator. As everyone knows, car simulators are not very popular in the gaming industry. The second reason is that we want to see your feedback and plan a future game together.[/i]

[b]Why the answer to many requests is “no, we won’t have it”?[/b]
[i]The type of the game has already been planned, so at the moment, we are creating the foundation for the future. We collect all reviews: about the drunk driver mode, and about Russia, and about traffic rules in the UK.[/i]

[b]What about the graphics?[/b]
[i]We have optimized the game for different devices. For example, the teaser was shot on “default” settings, not even on medium graphics settings. Since then, it has changed for the better. We constantly share the look of the game “at the moment,” so before the game is released in early access, we will definitely preview the final look of the graphics.[/i]

[b]Why are logs published only once every two weeks, and video formats, even short ones, have appeared not long ago?[/b] 
[i]We do not have a development or marketing team. All videos and screenshots are taken during the work of level designers. Most of the logs, which do not touch on a serious technical component, are written by our game designer. The tester carefully reads all the errors, and the project manager tries not to lose the semantic component by reading the log again before publication. We do all the logs in between our main work sessions.[/i]

[h2]What’s next?[/h2] 
We are finishing up the location, straightening up the gameplay, testing traffic, and finalizing the weather.

After that, we carefully polish the game for the remaining time and release it in early access. Part of the team, when they complete work on early access, will move on to creating the second half of the city, creating new game modes and tasks.

What we tell in the logs before the game release in early access is certainly not everything we planned. 
At the end of the log, we would like to specifically note that we see and collect all feedback and try to personally answer every question and comment. And you can also influence the game and its final appearance after early access.

notes.title: Developers diaries #12
notes.content:
Pedestrians have changed the most compared to the original CCD. In the teaser, which everyone is already familiar with, we used exported models from Fuse: for the chosen setting, pedestrians required different clothes, and the quality of the model was approximately at the level of the original CCD.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/8f69900856d9d45f474da0f6e2a7d5f48741f652.png[/img]
At the same time, we realized that this level of model implementation, though perhaps the best for optimization, fails to meet the modern quality standard for games. In turn, UE has its own, quite handy character creation tool – MetaHuman.

For CCD 2.0 in MetaHuman, we create only the basic proportions of pedestrians’ bodies and their faces. After that, the artists perform a retopology of the model, which contributes to our goals for optimizing the game. Hair and clothing are created as separate models in the appropriate software and assembled with human models from MetaHuman. After that, all pedestrians are loaded into UE and used in CCD 2.0.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/77cb3ea9995860656f6565592dd7e8126ca83957.png[/img][i]On the left is a pedestrian created using Fuse early in the game’s development. On the right, one created using MetaHuman[/i]

After a short excursion into exactly how new models are created, let’s turn our attention to the most important point: the gameplay. Pedestrians in CCD 2.0 have a number of differences from the original game.

The first major change is that pedestrians now have full-fledged physics. If you drive carelessly, pedestrians will jump away from your vehicle, or you may hit them. Fortunately, it’s not fatal. For such behavior and causing harm to pedestrians, players will be subject to appropriate punishment, which we will definitely talk about in our logs dedicated to the general pace of the game and the topic of compliance with traffic rules.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/31076b815c3823147d327a0675c39017bc46f5ab.png[/img]
The second change is related to the general atmosphere and mood of the game: pedestrians are true city residents, and not a decoration or an obstacle for you as a driver. For example, people in police uniforms will be located only near the police station, various workers, correspondingly, at construction sites. All this is also applied in the game modes of taxi driving and cargo courier. The final additional touch is that people will react to weather changes on the streets: pedestrians will mainly be dressed for the weather.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/f32eab75d29c7d333651d6af45035458a0444aa3.png[/img]
All vehicles in CCD 2.0 are completely new models: we decided not to carry over anything from CCD1 due to the fact that there is a strong visual difference between the current mode of transport and what we had. Some objects, such as tractors, can be occasionally found in the game world.

The main difference between traffic vehicles and the player’s cars is the detailing of the interior. For optimization purposes, the detailing of the interior in traffic vehicles has been simplified. The cars that you can drive have a very detailed interior shown right down to individual buttons. In early access, they will not be clickable, but we are building these features into the interior of the player’s car in advance.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/29985cc99646cd30c6ccc1750b8eedb146f548d7.png[/img]
In terms of the gameplay, cars are one of the main generators of all events in the game. All cars are full-fledged road users: they fully comply with traffic rules, can drive into parking spaces and create dangerous situations on the road. Traffic vehicles do not include heavy trucks or construction machines. However, you can see ambulances and police cars on the roads. In early access, we do not implement all the planned functionality associated with these vehicles, so we note just their presence, but not the implementation of all the planned functionality. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/c281d65958c243f8151f28da528a3df99209c552.png[/img]

[b]Will there be economy and sport modes in cars?[/b]
[i]No, in early access, these driving modes will not be available on the cars that we are preparing for CCD 2.0[/i] 

[b]Will electric cars be available in the game?[/b]
[i]In early access, we focus on standard, familiar cars, and there will be no electric cars in early access. However, we do not rule out the addition of the increasingly popular electric car in the future, especially given the trend for the promotion of electric cars[/i]

[b]Will a drunk driver mode be added?[/b]
[i]As we have noted several times, CCD 2.0 is created more according to the patterns of a game rather than a training aid. Therefore, this idea was not included in CCD 2.0 initially. However, we see a demand for this rather popular mechanic, so after early access, in future updates, we will consider the possibility of adding such a function to the game[/i]

[b]What about the licensed car?[/b] 
[i]We have no ability to license vehicles. We try to implement all cars as realistically as possible and bring them as close to the original as possible. As regards the brand, patented objects and other technological features, CCD 2.0 won’t have them even after early access[/i]

[b]Do you plan a release on consoles, not just PCs?[/b]
[i]No, we don’t at the moment, but if City Car Driving 2.0 becomes a popular car simulator, then of course we would like to expand to these devices[/i]

[b]And what about cloud gaming?[/b]
[i]We don’t plan it at the moment either. This is also why we try to optimize the game for old and weak computer configurations[/i]

[b]Will there be microtransactions?[/b] 
[i]It’s the first question where our “no” will sound like something good. No, microtransactions are not planned and will not be available in CCD 2.0[/i]

[b]What are the plans for DLC?[/b]
[i]We have none now. Before we consider DLC, we should release the game in early access and then successfully bring it to full release and implement the full potential we planned for CCD 2.0[/i]

notes.title: Developers diaries #11
notes.content:
The dynamic weather system and the day/night cycle are key elements to creating an atmospheric and believable world. Such systems should generate not only interesting gameplay moments, but also aesthetic ones.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/ce0b345d6b113ac79aaf58b4108da66b65e7167c.png[/img]
Before embarking on such a big task, we need to answer the question, “What do we want to get?”

Firstly, the time of day and weather should influence the behavior of pedestrians, traffic, illumination with streetlights, the light in the windows of houses, and the controllability of the player’s car. This means that state changes should be stored in a place that can be easily accessed from the outside, and the necessary data can be retrieved at any time.

Secondly, all this should be visually displayed, and as close to reality as possible. For example, surfaces get wet when it rains, and remain wet for some time after the rain. Clouds smoothly cover the sky, causing shadows to disappear in more diffused light. And it should all look great at any time of the day.

Thirdly, it must be easily customizable, controllable, and scalable. We should be able to add new weather for future development of the project. Weather may also be required in certain game situations, which means it should be possible to change it from other classes.

Also, artists should have access to all the necessary parameters in one place to fine-tune the graphics.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/427f7453c40a7d86b1c801fa9c6e8e3e2913a93f.png[/img]
Okay, the goal has been set; what next?

To begin with, after looking at the points, you can exhale and easily throw away all thoughts about the system for calculating weather changes in relation to temperature, humidity, magnetic storms, and the fact that the player washed the car.

And, like other companies, we stick to the idea of a pre-set weather forecast. This way, we solve two problems at once: the need to create a heavy weather generation system and the fact that, with random generation, we may have conditions when the weather does not look attractive enough.

Next, you need to think about the architecture of this system. This is where block diagrams come in handy.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/bc42553f18bc92a0cbc4dc46bc5788bced7659b4.png[/img]
To maintain code purity and logic distribution, the entire system is divided into four Blueprint classes.
[list]
[*] [b]BP_PlanetTime[/b] — is responsible for the progress of the in-game time
[*] [b]BP_Biome[/b] — sets the basic settings of the level, its geographic coordinates, and possible weather
[*] [b]BP_WeatherSystem[/b] — calculates the current weather and transitions between its states
[*] [b]BP_LevelVisualization[/b] — accepts data from all three previous classes and, based on this data, sets the visualization[/list]
[h2]BP_PlanetTime[/h2]

This is a class whose responsibilities extend far beyond the weather system. Traffic, pedestrians, and even the clock on your phone should receive accurate time, know of the minutes that have passed, and some elements should be able to rewind time.

Interfaces are well suited for implementing such functionality. The time class at the start searches through interfaces, transmits a link to itself to everyone it finds, and at the time of the game it calls an event to which those elements that need it subscribe.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/7ec7e63dc1cf592adc4880e5b50ed275ec5ca4ad.png[/img]
Thus, each element will decide for itself whether it needs to do something after the event is called or not. And if it becomes necessary to stop the movement of time, we will have one entry point for this.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/a43467e96aad542273cfeda714b60338b3c7b7fe.png[/img]
The passage of time itself is implemented through a timer in Blueprints, where for each time it is called, the specified time is added, after which seconds, minutes, and hours are rounded. The resulting values are stored in a structure and can be retrieved by anyone who has a link to [b]BP_PlanetTime[/b].

Additionally, parameters are displayed for setting the game time, how many seconds, minutes, or hours pass in the game in a real second. Plus, functions have been introduced to stop, rewind, and get time in text format for the in-game clock.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/d70cb34218ba4a40cea6bf3845014b4b45351fe1.png[/img][i]Example of rounding minutes and call to check the state of the day (morning, afternoon, evening, and night)[/i]

[h2]BP_Biome[/h2]

This class is the easiest to implement; it specifies the values of latitude, longitude, and north offset at the level. Filters for possible weather in a given location can also be set here.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/d383cc006008eb9c97c4ed736a3147899c699e23.png[/img]

In terms of architecture, it also transmits a link to itself along with the data we specify.

[h2]BP_WeatherSystem[/h2]

This class must receive information from [b]BP_PlanetTime[/b] and [b]BP_Biome[/b], determine the weather state, and most importantly, implement transitions between them.

But where do we store all the weather information at every moment of every day? And do it so that all this is not constantly kept in the memory. Plus, the system should be easy to fill to quickly make a monthly forecast because we need to achieve visual diversity.

To solve these problems, a weather forecast was introduced, which stores a list of days, and each day already stores a set of time periods with their own weather values. Each period has a start and end time. There is also a standard state into which the weather will go if no weather forecast is found for some time.

It was decided to store the weather forecast in the Data Assets format. This is a way of storing data in Unreal Engine, including not only values, but also functions.

The first step is to create Primary Data Assets, which declares all the necessary variables and functions. And then, based on this, Data Assets are created to fill them with unique data.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/8a3f06de217b96d74be0785d22da5c94f41299a6.png[/img][i]Here is a function from Primary Data Assets to search for weather conditions by day and hour[/i]

But how many parameters will there be in the weather? Or rather, how long will it take to set them each time for all intervals for each day? Obviously, there will be more than one, which will take a lot of time. This is how the idea came to introduce weather presets, which would contain information about rain, cloudiness, getting wet, fog, etc. Data Assets were also used here.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/262c7d01f56a85179f8dddd2344a4d017a1436d2.png[/img][i]Example of weather presets created based on Primary Data Assets[/i]

All that remains is to resolve the issue of transitions between weather conditions. An instant transition is definitely not suitable, which means that for each time period we introduce the duration of the transition to a new state. But a linear transition will look boring, so we add a transition curve.

The curve should go from 0 to 1 in x and y, which allows it to be recalculated for any values, multiplying by the duration and by the delta between the initial and target values.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/86d35d2c516482952b3ab7a7669dc702a861d503.png[/img][i]The simplest transition curve between states[/i]

Only now, the transition from sunny weather to rain will consist of the simultaneous appearance of clouds and rain, which means we add a curve to each parameter inside the preset. This will allow us to set the clouds to appear quickly, with the rain appearing slowly.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/68631d8fe14cb6e29d9a6585aab73da9dd5d0148.png[/img][i]Macro transition between states inside [b]BP_WeatherSystem[/b][/i]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/d3693d313ca5d72da0f9488e13d355eb753226d7.png[/img][i]The function of transition between states within a weather preset[/i]

[h2]BP_LevelVisualization[/h2]

It is the simplest and most difficult class at once. In terms of architecture, it only receives data from all three previous classes and transmits them to visual components. The only thing that you need to do is to compare the output values of the weather state and the settings of clouds, particles, sky, and everything else. It’s so simple that a separate log will be written about it.

Thus, we have implemented dynamic weather, with the ability to flexibly configure all parameters, allowing you to get entirely different combinations and quickly make edits and settings.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/dd4b698f9666da306a5a5f3a25b042e6709e001b.png[/img]

notes.title: Developers diaries #10
notes.content:
In Developers diaries, we rarely describe the work on a project sequentially, from start to finish. 
Basically, we demonstrated various mechanics of the project: how they were made, what they look like, and how they will be played.

That’s why today’s episode will tell a little about how we started making CCD 2.0 in chronological order, without screenshots from the project in its current state. All materials used in these logs are materials accumulated during development.

[h2]Concept[/h2]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/51d41129f3069f15b11727f20495fa09b322146d.png[/img][i]One of the oldest game screenshots of the CCD 2.0 prototype. We called it Pilot Location then[/i]

It took some time for the idea of creating a sequel to CCD to come into being. 
As we have said several times, the main activity of our company, Forward, is simulators and specialized software, and not full-featured games.

So for the original CCD, we only released patches and visual updates, while the main content was updated much less frequently. By the 2020s, City Car Driving was already a complete and full-featured product for us, so we stopped releasing updates on Steam.

Over several years that the project was running, we returned several times to the idea of developing CCD not only as a simulator but also as a game. 

Players who have been with us for a long time know that back in the 2010s, we wanted to create the Transporter – a game project focused more on entertainment rather than education.

At the stage of detailed concept and teaser presentation, we realized that we lacked certain skills and knowledge. It was highly likely that a bad product would be created, so we decided to abandon further work on the Transporter.

[h2]First Steps[/h2]

In the early 2020s, when the gaming industry technology was booming, we again returned to the idea of transforming CCD.

No decent competitor has appeared on the market over time, and the simulator literally required updates.

So we began testing various game engines, and Unreal Engine 4 turned out to be the most suitable for the project. We wrote about it in detail in the second log.

We decided on the basic concept and chose the engine. What to do next? We know well the full development cycle for a simulator, but how do we create a game correctly? The most obvious thing was to start with a prototype.

The first task, one might say the main idea of CCD 2.0, was to create a game with minimum system requirements no higher than the original City Car Driving at normal graphics settings. 

We realize that not everyone has powerful computers that many modern games require. So we set ourselves the goal of creating a modern project that is pleasant to be in and, at the same time, can work on most computers. 

It all started with the creation of a prototype of the project’s graphics at the pilot location. And the first point that we began to work on was vegetation as the most heavy graphic component.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/b9d0a64d7d8cf24ed8f2c16a6080ecd05ae0e282.png[/img][i]Part of the pilot location. As you can see, the grass, trees, road, and its transitions are made from scratch; however, they still have some of the visual style of the original City Car Driving.[/i]

After working with vegetation, we transferred some of the models from the original CCD to evaluate performance. 

Of course, in the final version of CCD 2, all models will be new, but at that time we needed fast results on Unreal Engine 4.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/3f50aa1bfa989b9814df52a8da72a09379b04428.png[/img][i]Cars transferred from CCD 1 to the Pilot Location[/i]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/7546db28fbbc884e557f55bbfb00e1f26888019c.png[/img][i]The Pilot Location at night[/i]

We worked on the pilot location for about a year. We tried different options and figured out what the graphics might look like and how quickly the game would run. We gradually mastered Unreal Engine.
Before starting work on CCD 2.0, we wanted to solve an important issue with the generation of terrain and roads.

In the pilot location, all the roads were made by the designers manually, but for a release project, this approach would have been too time-consuming. We needed a landscape generator.

Unfortunately, even an engine as advanced as Unreal Engine cannot provide the tools to generate the type of landscape we need – a combination of neat geometric shapes of the road network, with hills, fields, and rivers of the natural landscape.

However, we already had our own generator that created the terrain and roads for CCD. Within a few months, we were able to adapt the generator to UE, and nothing stopped us from creating large mixed urban/suburban locations.

[h2]Appearance of CCD 2.0[/h2]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/e6a95ec9cca34d37e3d5889ac23bba0833d9b39f.png[/img][i]One of the first screenshots of the future CCD 2.0[/i]

After we figured out the technology, we started developing the game concept. As you could understand from previous logs, we do not want to reveal specific mechanics, graphics, or vehicles ahead of time. So, here we outline the main ideas only: 

[list]
[*] Maintain the core gameplay of the original City Car Driving – safe driving in accordance with traffic rules. Make it interesting for both novice drivers, who are just learning to drive, and experienced drivers. 
[*] Focus on immersion without direct control of the character because, in a car simulator, the character is the player themselves.
[*] ncrease the size of the city, make it more similar to a real place: with its own history and associated architecture, different districts, and unique names. 
[*] Maintain communication with the audience: talk to you more, take note of ideas, and give honest answers regarding the project. 
[*] And finally, create a project whose functionality we can easily maintain and update, and implement both our own vision and some of the audience’s desires (yes, multiplayer, we remember you).
[/list]
With these ideas, we started developing the project. The work has been underway for a year and a half, and during this time CCD 2.0 has already been modified many times. You can see how the graphics changed at the end of the log, where we placed screenshots comparing the current level of graphics and what we started with.

We really want to create one of the best driving simulators on the market that brings real benefits to novice drivers, but is also a lot of fun for everyone.

notes.title: Developers diaries #9
notes.content:
In the original City Car Driving, passenger transportation is the second important game activity. Just like cargo transportation, taxi driving has been significantly changed.

Passenger transportation is available at any time in the game, but thanks to many new features, taxi driving has a slightly different pace of the game.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/1e6b64897f5cc91367b6559d3d59cdee43d13a80.png[/img]
To start taxi driving, you, as in the case of cargo transportation, just need to use the in-game phone. Differences in the game modes are already noticeable at this stage.

You have an application on your phone that is almost identical to real taxi booking and taxi driver applications. When you select this application, an interactive map of the city will appear on your phone, showing points with passengers.

For each passenger, the points to pick them up and to deliver are shown. In addition to these points, passenger rating will be shown. The rating is an indicator for you: which passengers are good and which are not; which will be easier or harder to deal with.

Each time you enter the taxi application, or complete an order, the location of customers will change. Unlike in the case of cargo transportation, you will not have the opportunity to choose your favorite route. For each new passenger transportation, it will be necessary to optimize and recreate the route.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/fcfb460d79aa87417677b5a3da54f961121ccfcf.png[/img]
In the first part of City Car Driving, passenger transportation was a full-fledged game mode, including due to such a parameter as “passenger mood”.

Thanks to your feedback and a lot of “how it works” guides from the community, we were able to take into account the errors in the implementation of the “passenger mood” mechanics in CCD2.

Now the system is implemented in the following way: each passenger has their own list of wishes and requirements. There are customers who are the least picky about your car. They practically do not react if you arrive in a damaged or dirty car, they do not care how long the trip lasted, and how many times you stopped at gas stations.

The mood counter is not as sensitive and does not cause you, for example, to lose all your trip progress if you do not turn on the turn signal when changing lanes.

Depending on the condition of your car, the style of the trip, as well as the passenger themselves, this parameter becomes more predictable at the beginning of the trip and clearly signals the actions that can and cannot be allowed in taxi driving.

If one may say so, now the parameter of mood has turned into a “difficulty curve” that is predictable and, most importantly, maintains interest.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/9b32130dc56d7ff86b03af6057e0b8ea5620d9cc.png[/img]
[i]Taking this opportunity, in the topic about taxi driving, we will show the answer to one of the many comments: “The roads in the city are not uniform and include not only narrow streets.”[/i]

As with cargo transportation, there are various taxi modifiers that influence driving. And it’s not just the mood and requirements. Here are some examples:
[list]
[*] The passenger asks to stick to the average speed X and drive at it until the end of the trip 
[*] The passenger asks to reduce the speed to X and drive at it until the end of the trip 
[*] The passenger asks to pass through certain sections of locations
[*] The passenger asks to stop at a certain place before reaching the final destination
[*] The passenger can ask to pick up other passengers
[/list]While it is clear how all the modifiers influence the game, the last one listed should be reviewed in more detail.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/244578ee4a63117cf1399ee7b87478e9366a4bc4.png[/img]
In CCD 2.0, taxi driving is no longer limited to one passenger. Now you can choose a car for several passengers and pre-select orders with more than one customer. In this option, the mood counter is kept as one, but takes into account the desires of each passenger. Often, if you take an order for several people, several points appear at once where each person should be delivered.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/bbb323201692207411b18548b5432d3ecef7fe58.png[/img]
[i]Work on the location is not yet fully completed. For example, our embankment is not ready. The entire street is at the concept stage.[/i]

All mechanics in total provide a different experience than working as a courier to transport goods. In the taxi driver mode, your pace of the game increases, and the difficulty of completing the task grows. All this happens gradually, depending on your skills. This system provides a comfortable pace of the game for novice drivers, and a worthy challenge for experienced motorists.

Each of the game modes described above is designed to give you a different driving experience.

notes.title: Developers diaries #8
notes.content:
Today, let’s talk about delivery. In the original City Car Driving, this mechanics was one of the game’s two open-world activities. We’ve reworked delivery, turning it from a side activity into a full-fledged game mode. 

First of all, City Car Driving 2.0 is a game about driving a passenger car safely in urban settings. As we said earlier, there will be no trucks in the game. In contrast, the game will offer a variety of vans that can still be classified as passenger cars.

In a nutshell, delivery is a mode available in the game at any time. You have to deliver various goods from point A to point B.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/174166d520c4b3b18c54b7347ce97265afd68a62.png[/img]
To get started in the delivery business, all you have to do is go to the in-game phone and choose to work as a delivery driver. You will have a list of orders that need to be fulfilled.

Every time you want to take a job, the order list is randomly generated anew, so the delivery points are often different. However, if you wish to always drive on the same route when working as a delivery driver, the game gives you this opportunity.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/c00a0f781819ce7c4b9698766da4d0e2a9f9b258.png[/img]
Each cargo is a unique resource – small decorative objects; tools; anything that can be delivered on a vehicle not designed to carry cargo. In this mode, you play as a delivery driver rather than a trucker.

Each item has its delivery requirements. For example, decorative wood products can be delivered in any vehicle. Power generators, however, can only be delivered in a pickup truck or van. There’s no room for such resources in a sedan, and it’s not safe. ;(

Every resource has such delivery requirements.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/3341edee3c4bced58a82cdde1fbcefe8b2540124.png[/img]
Besides the mechanics of directly interacting with vehicles, the game map has special buildings, which can be called “merchants” for convenience. Each merchant only gives out their own kind of resource.

For example, a sawmill only provides wood products. Each merchant, in turn, also requires a certain resource. For example, the sawmill needs tools to work with wood. There are also merchants that provide all kinds of resources at once.

This system will help you build a variety of routes to fulfill delivery orders.  

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/d268e970acf251bf089ed0cb9d868caf6554b64c.png[/img]
It is not only resources that are characterized by their demanding delivery requirements. In City Car Driving 2.0, cars differ from each other more than by design and physical parameters.

Each car in the game will have its own load capacity, allowing you to adapt to each delivery order by changing your vehicle.

You will also be able to take an order where you need to deliver more goods than your vehicle can accommodate. That’s okay – you can complete the order in a few trips.
 
The system offers tremendous creative scope in fulfilling each order.
 
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/95cb1eaef7574586e7902db1b369c5e27aec2d31.png[/img]
All of the above are mostly preparations. Without them, the basic gameplay loop in the original City Car Driving was almost the same: you deliver a set of goods from point A to point B for as long as you like.

To spike more interest, this mode is now enhanced with game modifiers. The modifiers are additional trip complications designed to create unique situations when playing the game.
 
The first modifier found throughout the game is the timer. We understand that for many this is an annoying mechanics: for this reason, City Car Driving 2.0 countdown does not apply to every delivery.

You will always be alerted to the order requirements. Then there is the number of destinations. Before or during a trip, the order may change, and you may have to deliver goods to several places at once.
 
We still recommend you to be careful while fulfilling the order, albeit in-game – each goods have their own damage scale, and while iron items are mostly harmless, fine tools can be damaged.

All these mechanics, in our opinion, create a unique system, equally educating and allowing every car lover to enjoy the game.



[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/e1587d01f1caf24e0bcc3396dce0d9b36a70038a.png[/img]
In the next log, let’s not go too far afield and talk about driving a taxi.

notes.title: Developers diaries #7
notes.content:
This time we will be covering gameplay only. As we have stated many times, we are making a game, not an end-to-end tutorial, and a game requires smooth transition between learning and entertainment.

In CCD 2.0. this transition is implemented via specialized quests referred to as “Quest Exercises” by the development team. In our diary we will explain what these are, what inspired their creation, and for what purpose.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/56bc7474492071a51975e446beadf7f752d6ec93.png[/img]
At the stage of mechanics prototyping, we have decided to follow the path of CCD1, i.e., develop a set of motordrome quests of different difficulty levels. So, we start implementing mechanics of the quests with focus on the motordrome. After a few attempts, we realize that a city with a detailed environment and roads enables deployment of an interactive learning system.

This instigates us to look for solutions that answer the following key question: “How do we combine Safe Driving training quests and the city into a challenging yet educating experience?” This question together with the concept of “Random Events” from other open world games leads us to the idea of “Quest Exercises”.

Now during the game, you can discover unusual locations or events that stand out from usual behavior of pedestrian and car traffic. In most cases, these locations or events trigger a quest as you approach them. Unlike motordrome exercises, you have to look for these quests on your own. At times, it can be quite challenging.

Each of the quests has a unique set of exercises to test your skills.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/203ea0e79b367b6776d1f483be0a04a64d993a84.png[/img]
[i]Some requirements may include specific vehicle, such as quests that appear only if you are driving, e.g., a van.[/i]

For example, there is a quest that requires you to park your vehicle in a confined space hindered by pedestrians or passing vehicles. Another quest requires you to give a ride to a person along a high-traffic motorway at high velocity and with strict timer limits.

There is room for fun, too — in a location with an uphill road you are required to carry a box on the roof of your car without dropping it. For the purpose of learning, this quest tests your skills to control speed when driving uphill and to control cargo on the roof.

The closest equivalent of “Quest Exercises” are “Random Events” from other open world games. These served as inspiration for our team to develop the new gameplay element.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/083bf59c102f0e8b3fbc90bc3f8ee79c31c06509.png[/img]
[i]The quests are distributed around the game world, so we are just using this as an excuse to show you a parking space. Maybe one of the quests will take place here.[/i]

All quests you will find in the open world serve as an alternative to the tests and exercises in CCD1 Career mode. We find a combination of an interesting location and a quest more attractive than challenging motordrome exercises.

Quest Exercises implemented as discovery of the game world and delivered as optional activities are what, in our opinion, helps form a thrilling gameplay with an idea of learning at its foundation. This is why each completed quest gets you a score similar to that at the motordrome.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/b3ffaa2560fa2f0442d7bda6d213910739c25d4f.png[/img]
[i]Regardless of where the “Quest Exercise” starts, while on it, you also discover important city locations and learn its history.[/i]

The city (and even its central streets) is primarily made of narrow passages, roads, and crossroads. This type of city planning enables unique game experience and preserves integrity of the main idea of City Car Driving series. Maintaining balance is the key for each quest we develop. The idea would be probably best described as realistic, challenging, and interactive Safe Driving training.

We do not support the approach of “advanced outposts” or “map question marks” as we find it unsuitable for a driving simulator. However, we aim to deliver unique experience not only in the terms of Traffic Rules. Quest Exercises are an optional but critical game element that enables smooth transition from learning to entertainment via gameplay. We as a team of developers want you to discover the game on your own and choose the activities your find attractive.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/4c51f030f4b7426623bf4615a56e765fca9ec8a6.png[/img]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/c281d65958c243f8151f28da528a3df99209c552.png[/img]

[b]Why is Q&A missing from previous Developers Diaries?[/b]
[i]We answer all your questions in the diaries. Since we had no new questions last time, we skipped Q&A section.[/i]

[b]Is voice navigation to be expected?[/b]
[i]We understand this is an important and interesting feature of a gameplay, however, this is not to be expected for early access.[/i]

[b]Do you plan additional traffic lights sections?[/b]
[i]These are implemented in CCD2.0[/i]

[b]Can you upload your own music to listen on the radio in the game?[/b]
[i]Yes, we believe this is important for full game world experience.[/i]

[b]Will we see construction works on the roads?[/b]
[i]Yes, but we are not ready to disclose the details yet.[/i] 

[b]What about a game demo?[/b]
[i]Highly unlikely.[/i] 

[b]When will the game be released?[/b] 
[i]We are not announcing the exact date to avoid disappointment in case of delays. The game will be released for early access somewhere in Q1 2024.[/i] 

[b]Why does the graphics look cartoon-like?[/b]
[i]The screenshots we use in Developers Diaries come directly from the engine at the moment the new diary is being written, without any rendering or color adjustment, so these screenshots do not represent the final graphics and are being continuously improved.[/i] 

[b]Why are streets so clean and perfect?[/b]
[i]o	Cracks, rubbish, dirt, etc. are final outcomes of level art. Currently, we are working on the contents of locations, and after this is finished, we will proceed to the details.[/i]



[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44086444/e1587d01f1caf24e0bcc3396dce0d9b36a70038a.png[/img]
In the next diary we will tell you about the most challenging and interesting game mechanics, which is transportation of cargo. This has been thoroughly reworked compared with the original CCD.
